title: What to Include in a Plumbing SEO Scope
html:
Use this guide to define a plumbing SEO scope and compare proposals. For Wonderweb deliverables and a project discussion, visit our plumbing SEO services page.

Define the plumbing work you want to win

Start with your actual service area and the jobs you can deliver. Emergency repairs, drain cleaning, water heaters and larger replacement work can need different information and response arrangements. Give the agency an approved service list, coverage boundaries, working hours and any capacity limits. The scope should explain which priorities will be addressed first and why.

Ask for a baseline and a prioritized audit

Request a review of important service pages, search visibility, indexing, mobile usability and inquiry delivery. Give each finding a priority, an owner and a proposed fix. Separate the time spent investigating from the time needed to implement changes. A useful audit explains the business consequence of an issue instead of presenting a long list of automated warnings.

Specify the content deliverables

Agree how many pages will be created or revised and who provides technical plumbing knowledge, photographs and project details. A water-heater page should explain the work you actually offer and how to request help. Specify research, writing, review rounds, publishing and internal links. Location pages should add useful local information; repeating the same page with a different town name is not a substitute for relevant content.

Keep business information accurate

For an eligible Google Business Profile, include a review of categories, service area, contact details and hours. State who owns the profile and who approves changes. Review requests should be part of a consistent customer follow-up process. Do not describe a remote marketing provider as a local plumbing office, or add locations the plumbing business does not operate.

Separate implementation from recommendations

Find out whether the monthly fee includes developer time, redirects, form repairs, performance work and ongoing site maintenance. Record exclusions such as hosting, photography and third-party subscriptions. A report that recommends a repair and a scope that includes delivering that repair are different commitments. Ask how the team verifies completed work and handles changes outside the agreed allowance.

Define what the report will measure

Agree how calls, forms, qualified inquiries, estimates and sold jobs are recorded. Search visibility and traffic can provide context, while your sales records help show whether inquiries fit the business. Check that tracking is working before relying on it. Ask the agency to explain the period, comparison and limitations of each result, including situations where a sale cannot be attributed confidently to one channel.

Compare proposals on ownership and scope

Compare the same deliverables, review frequency, implementation allowance and exclusions. Confirm that you retain access to your website, domain, business profile and analytics accounts. Record the cancellation process, content ownership and handover responsibilities. Costs depend on the website and work required; a fixed fee alone does not tell you whether two proposals offer the same service.

Set a review point without promising rankings

Agree when to review completed work, early signals and the next priorities. Search performance depends on the market, the website and factors outside an agency's control. Treat a timetable as a delivery and review plan, not a guaranteed ranking or lead-cost outcome. Bring your service list and current website to the first conversation so the proposal can address a concrete business problem.
